A. Learning a knot and delivering bread

Learning a knot from pictures can be surprisingly confusing. The rope in your hands may not seem to match the tidy lines on the page. Before abandoning the instructions, try changing the way you use them.

Choose a short piece of rope that is easy to handle. If the directions show two colours, use two colours yourself when possible. ____1____ You can then follow the same end through several pictures without losing track of it.

Place the instructions beside your hands, facing the same way as the demonstration. ____2____ A loop that appears on the left in the drawing should appear on your left too, unless the directions say otherwise.

Work through one movement at a time. Stop after each picture and compare the crossing points. ____3____ Pulling everything tight too soon can hide the point where your rope took a different path.

Once the knot looks correct, loosen it and try again. Keep the pictures nearby but look at them only when you need help. ____4____ Repeating the whole sequence helps connect the separate movements into a useful skill.

Finally, remember that a practice knot is not proof that you can use it safely for any purpose. ____5____ For climbing or carrying a heavy load, get suitable instruction and have the equipment and knot checked by someone qualified.

B. Learning a knot and delivering bread

Every Saturday, my neighbour makes bread for a small community breakfast. Last week, she invited me ____1____ (help) with the delivery. The loaves had cooled on wooden shelves, and the room was filled ____2____ the smell of warm flour.

Before ____3____ (pack) them, we checked a list of orders. Each bag needed a name because several people had requested different kinds of bread. I wrote the labels as ____4____ (clear) as I could and placed the finished bags beside the door.

One customer, ____5____ house was at the end of our street, had asked us to leave her order with a neighbour. She had written the arrangement on the form, so we did not need to guess what to do if she was out.

The bags ____6____ (carry) to the breakfast hall in two large boxes. I walked beside my neighbour, holding the lighter one. When we arrived, some ____7____ (volunteer) were setting the tables while others checked the kitchen.

It was such ____8____ busy morning that I hardly noticed the time. Yet nobody hurried me when I asked where a bag should go. The route became ____9____ (easy) to remember than it had been at first. By noon, we had delivered all the bread and washed the empty boxes. My neighbour thanked me for giving up part of ____10____ (I) weekend.

originalGroup.material:
A. Borrowing a telescope and recording plants

A borrowed telescope may offer an exciting first view of the night sky. It also comes with controls that an experienced owner uses almost without thinking. A useful handover gives the borrower a chance to understand those controls before the first dark evening.

Ask the owner to demonstrate setting it up in daylight. Find out which parts must be secured and which are meant to move. ____1____ That distinction prevents a natural attempt to adjust the view from loosening something important.

Try repeating the setup while the owner watches. A demonstration can seem obvious until you have to choose the next action yourself. ____2____ Ask about any step at which you are relying on a guess.

Agree on a simple first target and suitable viewing conditions. Searching at random can be frustrating when you are still learning to aim. ____3____ The Moon, when appropriately visible, may be easier to find than a faint object among many stars. Never point a telescope at the Sun without proper specialist solar equipment and guidance.

Find out how to pack the instrument after use. ____4____ A photograph of the correctly arranged case can be more helpful than trying to remember where every small part belongs.

Finally, settle practical details about returning it. ____5____ If the weather prevents your planned evening, contact the owner rather than assuming you may keep the instrument longer. Clear arrangements protect both the equipment and the relationship.

B. Borrowing a telescope and recording plants

Our class was invited to record the plants in a roof garden. The gardener gave us a map ____1____ showed the different beds, but she warned us that the list of names was not completely up to date. Some plants had been moved since it was drawn.

After ____2____ (divide) into pairs, we chose one bed each. My partner and I decided ____3____ (begin) with the labels rather than trying to identify everything from memory. We copied the names and noted whether a label was missing or ____4____ (damage).

There were more pots than we had expected. To avoid counting one twice, we moved ____5____ (slow) along a row and marked its end on the map. We also took photographs, making sure that each one could be linked to a particular position.

At the end, the gardener thanked us ____6____ our careful notes. She did not treat every copied name as a confirmed identification. Instead, the uncertain entries ____7____ (check) against her planting records the following day.

The task taught me that a useful record needs more than a neat appearance. Its limits must be described as ____8____ (careful) as its findings. We added a short explanation of ____9____ we had done, including the date and the beds we had covered. That made it easier for another group to continue without ____10____ (repeat) all our work.

originalGroup.material:
A. Reading subtitles and preserving labels

Subtitles can make a film accessible across languages, yet they cannot reproduce every feature of a conversation. Speech, images and written lines operate together. Understanding that relationship helps viewers read a subtitle as a considered representation rather than a complete transcript.

Notice how much can appear on screen at once. A speaker may talk faster than a viewer can comfortably read. ____1____ Reducing the wording can preserve the main point while leaving time to watch the scene.

Consider information carried by the image. If a character is visibly pointing at a broken chair, a subtitle may not need to repeat every descriptive word. ____2____ What is omitted from the text may still be communicated clearly by another channel.

Be cautious when judging a phrase in isolation. A short reply can express agreement, doubt or irritation depending on the voice and preceding exchange. ____3____ Reading only a screenshot can remove exactly the evidence that made the choice appropriate.

Recognise that some choices involve a trade-off. A joke based on a particular sound may not work in another language. ____4____ Neither choice preserves every feature, so the purpose of the scene matters.

Finally, distinguish a genuine error from a choice you would have made differently. ____5____ Looking at that evidence makes criticism more precise and gives due attention to the constraints under which the line was written.

B. Reading subtitles and preserving labels

While sorting the papers in a community garden shed, I found a box of seed labels. They came from a gardener ____1____ had worked there before I joined. Some were still easy to read; others had faded almost completely.

I wanted to replace them. But the current gardener suggested ____2____ (keep) the originals until we had recorded their information. An uncertain word should not become a confident guess because it was copied ____3____ (neat).

We photographed each label beside a ruler, then gave the image a number. The number was linked to the bed ____4____ which the label had been found. Where a plant name was unclear, we described the uncertainty instead of supplying one from memory.

Several earlier photographs ____5____ (store) in a folder on the garden computer. Comparing them with our images helped us read two faded names. It also reminded us that a plant could have been moved since a picture was taken.

The final list contained fewer confirmed ____6____ (name) than I had hoped. Nevertheless, it was ____7____ (reliable) than a complete list based on guesses. We decided ____8____ (add) new observations as the plants developed, rather than pretending the work was finished.

Only after the record was complete ____9____ we put the labels into protective envelopes. Their handwriting was worth keeping. It was part of the garden's history, and we had a ____10____ (responsible) to preserve it.
